title: The skilled driver
theme: For one with understanding, whose mind is always held, the senses obey, like a good driver’s good horses.

sandhi.rule: Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
āḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus remains.

morphology.note: vijñāna with the possessive suffix -vat, nominative singular masculine -vān.
sat ‘good’ before a vowel keeps its d (sad-aśva) in the compound.

translation.literal: ‘But he who is possessed of understanding, with a mind always held — his senses are controllable, like the good horses of a charioteer.’
translation.readable: ‘When the driver has understanding and always holds the mind steady, the senses obey, like a good driver’s well-trained horses.’

anvaya: यः तु विज्ञानवान् सदा युक्तेन मनसा भवति, तस्य इन्द्रियाणि सारथेः सदश्वाः इव वश्यानि [भवन्ति] ॥
syntax: The exact counterpart of 1.3.5: a relative clause with tasya as correlative, and a nominal main clause with the simile sadaśvā iva sāratheḥ. Each negative of 1.3.5 (avijñānavān, ayuktena, avaśyāni, duṣṭāśvāḥ) is here positive.

ambiguities.topic: Control as restraint and as use
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: ‘controllable’ means the senses can be set going or held back, «प्रवर्तयितुं निवर्तयितुं वा शक्यानि»; the verse does not ask that they be stopped, only that they answer to the driver.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: 17 and 16 syllables: the first pāda, yas tu vijñānavān bhavati, has nine. In 1.3.5 the vowels of tu and bhavati fuse with the following a- (yas tv avijñānavān bhavaty ayuktena), which keeps that pāda at eight; here there is no such junction.

beginner: This verse is the mirror of the one before it. Now picture a driver who knows the road and keeps a steady hold on the reins. The horses are strong — they have not changed — but they go where they are directed. In the same way, when a person's understanding is clear and the mind is held steady, the senses do what is asked of them. Śaṅkara points out that 'controlled' does not mean switched off: the senses can be sent forward or held back as needed, like horses that can be urged on or reined in. The good driver is not one with weaker horses, but one with a better grip. Read together, the two verses say that the same energies can carry us well or badly, depending on who holds the reins.
analogy: Like a rider on a spirited horse who has trained it well: the strength is the same as a runaway’s, but it carries the rider where she means to go.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That for one with understanding and a mind always held, the senses are under control, like the good horses of a charioteer.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: This is the reward of the opposite kind of charioteer, «पूर्वोक्तविपरीतसारथिर्भवति तस्य फलमाह»: the one who is skilled and discerning, «निपुणः विवेकवान्», with the mind held and settled, «प्रगृहीतमनाः समाहितचित्तः», has senses that can be set going or held back, like tamed good horses, «दान्ताः सदश्वा».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: His joint comment on 1.3.5–6: when understanding and mind, the charioteer and reins, are sound, the senses, the horses, are under control, «अश्वत्वेन रूपितानि इन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि भवन्ति».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

advaita.text: The skilled charioteer’s senses can be set going or held back at will, «प्रवर्तयितुं निवर्तयितुं वा शक्यानि».

visistadvaita.text: Control of the senses follows from sound understanding and mind, as horses obey a good charioteer: «अश्वत्वेन रूपितानि इन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि भवन्ति».

schools.disagreement: No disagreement between Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja on this verse. In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

contemporary.text: Discipline here is not suppression but skill: the horses keep all their strength. That is a useful corrective to the idea that self-control means doing less. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: Where in your life do your senses already ‘obey’ you well?
reflect.deeper: What is the difference, in Śaṅkara’s gloss, between controlling the senses and stopping them?
reflect.practice: Do one ordinary task today with full attention to it alone.

flags.note: madhva.json files Madhva’s single comment on 1.3.10–11 (his mark ॥ १०-१२ ॥) under every mantra from 1.3.3 to 1.3.11; it is not quoted here.
